paras: The threatened lynching of George W. Blanchard was a disturbance in the Criminal Court of the District of Columbia in Washington on January 17, 1888, in which spectators shouted "lynch him" and "string him up" and rushed at Blanchard, a traveling showman, after a jury acquitted Bessie (Elizabeth) Morrison of stealing $697 from him. Blanchard got away without any reported injury, by running into the street in one local account and with the help of a police officer in another. Two Washington papers headlined the scene, and a short wire version ran in Connecticut and Michigan.

Morrison, a young woman whose family lived near Ishpeming, Michigan, was charged with the larceny of $697 from Blanchard, alias D. W. Donaldson, at Richmond, Virginia, on December 14, 1887, and had been arrested in Baltimore. At the trial before Justice Montgomery, defense counsel Campbell Carrington told the jury that Blanchard had drawn her from home to join a show of "a few monkeys, freaks" and other acts, had "accomplished her ruin" under a promise of marriage, and had told her that all he had was hers. Blanchard denied any promise of marriage; the case went to the jury without argument, and the verdict of not guilty came within five to ten minutes.

Applause met the verdict and grew when the jury foreman asked that the $697 be given to Morrison and the court ordered it returned to her. After the judge left the bench, jurors and spectators crowded around Morrison to congratulate her, and Blanchard pushed close, took hold of her sleeve or arm, and said he wanted to talk with her. In the National Republican's version, Carrington ordered him to leave the courtroom "or we will string you up," and the crowd took up the words with cries of "hang him," "lynch him" and "string him up" and made a rush for him.

The Evening Star quoted Carrington as telling Blanchard to "go home and look after your monkeys" or be strung up, after which someone cried "Hang the d————!" and many in the crowd made for Blanchard, "almost lifting him from his feet." On his escape, the Republican said he was pursued by "the infuriated people" and lost sight of on Pennsylvania avenue, while the Star said Officer McTaggert and others seized him and hustled him from the room, "saving him from the fury of the crowd."

About fifty people, the jurors at their head, escorted Morrison to Carrington's office in the Republican's account, or to police headquarters, where the money was returned, in the Star's. Spectators waiting outside the office said he "deserved a coat of tar and feathers" and seemed willing to help apply it. According to the Star, Morrison left on an evening train for her home in Michigan. No report of an arrest appears in the coverage.

The Washington evening papers of January 17 covered the trial the same day, the Washington Critic as "Dazzled by the Spangles," without mentioning a disturbance; the Star noted only "suppressed applause." The next morning the National Republican printed the fullest account under the headline "Bessie Found Friends Through the Evil Deeds of a Bad Showman Being Made Public," with a deck reading "Blanchard Runs to Escape the Crowd." That afternoon the Star followed with "They Threatened Lynching," while its court column listed the case only as a larceny ending in a verdict of not guilty.

Both local papers told the story from Morrison's side, describing Blanchard twirling his silk hat while she cried; neither criticized the crowd. A brief wire dispatch dated January 18 ran in the Waterbury Evening Democrat that day under "Her Deceiver and Persecutor Flies to Escape Rough Treatment," and in Michigan's Telegram-Herald on January 19 as "Shouts of Lynch Him." The Richmond Dispatch reprinted the Republican's account on January 19 under the headline "Singular Scenes in Court. Where Much Chivalry is Shown a Wayward Woman."
Later notices, in a Baltimore German-language paper and a Michigan weekly, mentioned only the acquittal.

Besides the escape, the accounts differ on timing: the wire placed the cries at the verdict itself, while both Washington papers, which gave fuller accounts, placed them after Carrington's remark to Blanchard.

bases: After an acquittal, a courtroom crowd shouted 'lynch him' and rushed at the complaining witness, who escaped unhurt; no seizure, rope or injury is reported (A5, A7).
No one was killed: a crowd threatened to hang Blanchard and rushed him, but he escaped or was led out by an officer (A5, A7).
Two independent local reports (A5, A7) and a wire dispatch (A8, A9) agree that the crowd cried 'lynch him' or 'hang' and went for Blanchard, though they differ on details of his escape.
